plain_title: Repeated movements that are hard to stop and can cause harm
one_liner: Repetitive, rhythmic, seemingly purposeless movements, like rocking or hand-flapping, that interfere with life or cause injury.
in_simple_words: Many children rock, flap, or twirl, especially when excited, and most of the time that's harmless and normal. Stereotypic movement disorder is diagnosed when repetitive movements take up so much time that they get in the way of play, learning, or daily life, or when they cause injury, like head-banging. It's more common in children with intellectual disability or autism. Care focuses on safety, understanding what the movement does for the child, and gentle ways to reduce harm.
what_it_can_feel_like: Hand-flapping is how my body says happy. The only problem was other people's faces.
His head-banging terrified us. The team helped us see what he was trying to tell us.
I rock when I think. I'm 40 and I've stopped apologizing for it.
common_signs: Repetitive, rhythmic movements: rocking, hand-flapping, waving, head-banging, hitting or biting oneself
Movements that start in early childhood and seem to have no purpose
Movements that take up a lot of time or interrupt activities
In some children, movements that cause bruising, wounds, or other injury

myths_vs_facts.myth: All repetitive movements need to be stopped.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Harmless stereotypies, including most autistic stimming, help with regulation and don't need treatment. Only movements that interfere or injure are a disorder.
Self-injurious movements usually serve a function, such as relieving pain, distress, or overload, or communicating a need. Finding the function is the key to helping.
Behavioural and environmental approaches come first. Medication is sometimes used for severe self-injury, prescribed and monitored by a specialist.

how_common.plain: Simple stereotypies are common in young children. The disorder itself is uncommon in typically developing children and much more common in children with intellectual disability, especially severe disability.
how_common.figure: DSM-5-TR text: simple stereotypies common (3–4% of young children); self-injurious stereotypies in about 4–16% of people with intellectual disability, higher with greater severity
how_common.note: Figures from the DSM-5-TR text; needs a primary source.

what_helps.plain_summary: The first step is a careful assessment of when the movement happens and what it achieves for the child, often by a behaviour specialist. Treatment then uses environmental changes, teaching other ways to meet the same need, and safety measures like protective equipment where needed. Any pain or medical cause is treated. For severe self-injury, medication may be considered, prescribed and monitored by a specialist. For harmless stereotypies, the best treatment is acceptance.
evidence_based_options: Functional behavioural assessment and behaviour support plans
Treating pain, discomfort, or medical causes
Medication in some cases of severe self-injury, prescribed and monitored by a specialist
self_help_that_supports_care: Keeping a diary of when movements happen and what came before
Offering safe sensory alternatives: chewable jewellery, cushions, movement breaks
Support for carers, as this can be frightening and exhausting

when_to_reach_out: If a child's repetitive movements are causing injury, stopping them from playing or learning, or are new or sudden, ask a doctor for an assessment. Sudden onset of self-injury can signal pain or illness and needs checking.
is_not: Stimming in autistic people that doesn't cause harm is not a disorder and shouldn't be treated as one. Tics are faster, less rhythmic, and preceded by an urge. Compulsions in OCD are done on purpose to relieve anxiety. Trichotillomania and skin-picking have their own diagnoses.
hope_note: When the reason behind a movement is understood, families and teams can find safer ways to meet the need, and children can keep the comfort without the harm.
in_young_people: Stereotypies usually begin before age three. In typically developing children they often fade; in children with developmental disabilities they may persist and need ongoing support.

content_notes: Mentions self-injury in a developmental context, without method detail. Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.
